after: ## 8.1 Why was there such dissatisfaction with the peace settlements?
alt: Three cards. Clemenceau wanted security: reparations, disarmament and a Rhineland buffer. Lloyd George wanted Germany punished but able to trade, with British naval and imperial interests protected. Wilson wanted self-determination, open diplomacy and a League. Below: the defeated powers and Soviet Russia had no voice, and smaller allies little say.
caption: Three different aims produced compromises that satisfied no one fully.

after: ## 8.1 Why was there such dissatisfaction with the peace settlements?
alt: Eight cards. France thought the treaty too lenient and lost its guarantee; Britain had doubts, encouraged by Keynes; the USA refused to ratify; Italy spoke of a mutilated victory; Japan gained Shandong but had its racial equality clause rejected; Germany called it a Diktat; Russia was excluded. A final card notes that self-determination was applied inconsistently.
caption: Every power, winners included, found something to resent.

after: ## 8.2 Why was the League created and what challenges did it face?
alt: An organisation chart: the Assembly of all members; the Council with permanent members Britain, France, Italy and Japan; the Secretariat in Geneva; and the Permanent Court at The Hague. Below, five agencies (refugees, ILO, slavery, disarmament, mandates) and the League's weaknesses: restricted membership, unanimous voting, no army and divided leadership.
caption: A full structure, but no army and decisions that needed unanimity.

after: ## 8.2 Why was the League created and what challenges did it face?
alt: Six disputes ranked from most to least effective: the Aaland Islands (ruling accepted), the Greco-Bulgarian border (success against a small power), Upper Silesia (a compromise), Teschen (decided by the Conference of Ambassadors), Memel (a fait accompli accepted) and Vilna (seized by Poland, which kept it).
caption: The League worked when both sides accepted a ruling, or the aggressor was small.

after: ## 8.3 Why did tensions remain high after Versailles?
alt: A vertical timeline from 1919 to 1930 drawn to scale. Before 1924 most events are crises: Fiume, the Little Entente, Rapallo, the Ruhr occupation (January 1923) and Corfu. From 1924 most are co-operation: the Dawes Plan, Locarno (1925), Germany joining the League (1926), Kellogg-Briand (1928) and the Young Plan (1929), until Stresemann's death and the Crash in October 1929.
caption: Crises cluster before 1924; agreements cluster after it.

after: ## 8.4 How and why did relations improve, 1924-29?
alt: A labelled schematic, not a map. Germany sits between France and Belgium on one side and Poland and Czechoslovakia on the other. The western border is drawn as a solid line, accepted by Germany and guaranteed by Britain and Italy; the eastern border is a dashed line, covered only by arbitration treaties.
caption: Locarno settled Germany's western borders but left the eastern ones open.

alt: A pyramid of three layers. At the top, Locarno (1925), which made improvement visible. In the middle, the Dawes Plan (1924), the Stresemann-Briand partnership and exhaustion after the Ruhr, which made it possible. At the base, American loans, which were recalled after the Wall Street Crash.
caption: Locarno sat on the Dawes Plan, and both sat on American loans.
